comments.text: Y aún hay más: la historia del Gaucho Rivero. Los invito a viajar en el tiempo a través de estas líneas para conocer una de las paradojas legales e históricas más asombrosas del siglo XIX: la historia de Antonio "El Gaucho" Rivero. Es la crónica de una rebelión, un inesperado vacío legal y el dilema de un imperio atrapado en sus propias leyes. Todo comenzó en enero de 1833, cuando el Reino Unido invadió por la fuerza las Islas Malvinas y expulsó a las autoridades argentinas. Un grupo de indefensos trabajadores criollos e indígenas permaneció en el lugar. Las nuevas autoridades británicas comenzaron a aplicar un régimen de explotación insostenible. A los gauchos se les prohibió estrictamente izar la bandera argentina y, para colmo, se les pagaba por su arduo trabajo con vales de la anterior administración argentina, que el comerciante local se negaba a aceptar para venderles alimentos y ropa. Hartos del hambre y el desprecio, el 26 de agosto de 1833, el gaucho Rivero lideró a un grupo de ocho hombres en una audaz rebelión. Ejecutaron a los capataces británicos, arriaron su bandera e izaron el estandarte que defendían, tomando el control de las islas durante meses. Una fragata llegó para capturarlos. Rivero y sus hombres fueron encadenados y trasladados a Inglaterra para ser juzgados por asesinato en el tribunal de Portsmouth. El imperio buscaba un castigo ejemplar, pero ahí es donde se produjo el giro más sorprendente de esta historia. No tenían jurisdicción para juzgarlos porque no existían las Cartas Patentes. Para que un tribunal inglés juzgara un delito colonial, la Corona debía haber emitido las credenciales legales que establecían formalmente un gobierno civil y un sistema judicial local. En ese momento, el Reino Unido no tenía Cartas Patentes sobre las Malvinas; solo poseía un territorio recientemente tomado por la fuerza militar. Los jueces entendieron que, si seguían adelante con el juicio sin esas credenciales, quedarían expuestos: estarían admitiendo ante el mundo entero que la Corona británica operaba fuera de sus propias leyes, juzgando un territorio sobre el cual legalmente no poseían títulos ni constituían soberanía. Para evitar la vergüenza internacional de confesar que las islas eran, según su propia ley, un territorio usurpado sin base legal, el gobierno británico decidió no juzgarlos, liberarlos y devolverlos al Río de la Plata. El principal lugar físico y digital es el Archivo Nacional del Reino Unido ubicado en Kew, Londres. Documentos del Almirantazgo: Debe buscar en la serie de archivos identificados con el código ADM 1/44. Esta sección agrupa cartas, correspondencia y actas legales intercambiadas entre los Secretarios de Estado de la época (como Hammond y Hamilton) durante el año 1835, detallando la detención de los prisioneros a bordo del buque de guardia en Sheerness y los dilemas de los jueces. Bibliotecas de periódicos y prensa de la época: En la Biblioteca Británica,Dentro de sus archivos históricos de periódicos (British Newspaper Archive), las noticias del caso publicadas entre mayo de 1835 y los meses posteriores se pueden rastrear bajo palabras clave como "Antonio Rivero", "asesinos de las Islas Malvinas" o "HMS Snake" (el barco que completó el traslado de los detenidos al estuario del Támesis). Las crónicas portuarias y los periódicos locales de Portsmouth detallan la llegada de los "gauchos encadenados" y su posterior y misteriosa liberación sin condena

replies.author: @alnm951
replies.text:
@Wacko-_-Jackooo  The narrative you've presented is a selective reading of history that omits key legal facts and misrepresents the nature of sovereignty claims. First, Britain's victory at Trafalgar in 1805 was a naval battle against the French and Spanish fleets, but it did not establish British sovereignty over the Malvinas—sovereignty requires effective occupation and administration, not a military victory on the high seas. The claim that "the world knew Britain claimed sovereignty and respected it" is contradicted by the fact that Spain maintained exclusive control over the Malvinas from 1767 to 1811, with Britain recognizing Spanish sovereignty in the 1790 Nootka Convention and remaining completely silent for fifty years after abandoning Port Egmont in 1774.

Second, the claim that Vernet sought British "permission" misrepresents what actually occurred—Vernet's contact with the British Consulate was for routine administrative legalization of documents to attract European settlers, not a recognition of British sovereignty. He was officially appointed as Political and Military Commander of the Malvinas by the Buenos Aires government on 10 June 1829, and his settlement operated under Argentine laws, with Argentine currency, criminal proceedings, and national holiday celebrations, all without any British protest until later that year.

Third, the assertion that the USS Lexington attack and the Rivero mutiny somehow invalidate Argentina's sovereignty is legally irrelevant—states are not deprived of sovereignty by setbacks or internal incidents, and Britain's subsequent seizure in 1833 exploited a weakened colony rather than asserting any continuously maintained right. The 1833 seizure was an act of force against a friendly state with which Britain had a treaty of peace, and Argentina has continuously protested that seizure for nearly two centuries, preventing Britain from acquiring title by prescription.

Fourth, the fact that Vernet's enterprise included diverse nationalities does not undermine Argentina's claim—it actually proves that the settlement operated under Argentine authority, as all those individuals, regardless of origin, were subject to Argentine laws and governance. The presence of British sailors or German families does not make them representatives of British state authority; they were residents of an Argentine colony.

Finally, the argument that Argentina's sovereignty claim is "awful" because of these events ignores the established legal principles of uti possidetis iuris, state succession, and the prohibition on acquiring territory by force. Britain's title rests on a brief 18th-century settlement abandoned in 1774, followed by fifty years of silence and a forcible seizure in 1833 that has never been accepted by the dispossessed sovereign—and the UN has not recognized British sovereignty despite the century-long occupation. The UN continues to call for bilateral negotiation precisely because Argentina's claim remains legally valid under international law.

You are ignorant to the complex nature of geopolitics between 1750 and 1850. 

France, Britain and Spain raised their flag over the Falkland Islands before Argentina.

Britain destroyed both the French and Spanish (naval forces) in 1805 despite being outnumbered. Britain lost no ships during the battle of trafalgar. Britain was the reason that Spain had to abandon the Falkland Islands and South America in general. This ultimately lead to Argentina’s independence. The world knew that Britain claimed sovereignty to the Falkland Islands and respected it. 

Following Argentina’s independence (once acknowledged by Britain in 1825). Vernet (a German man whose lieutenant was British) actually approached the British Consulate in Buenos Aires before sailing. He secured their implicit consent to build a private enterprise, promising to send regular reports to London. However, when Buenos Aires later gave Vernet official political authority in 1829, Britain issued a formal diplomatic protest to protect its own sovereignty claim.

The population consisted of roughly 10 white Argentine citizens (spanish europeans), German and Dutch families, British sailors (including Vernet’s trusted lieutenant, Captain Matthew Brisbane), over 20 indentured Black labourers (former Spanish slaves) from Buenos Aires, and a handful of local indigenous people.

The downfall of Vernet’s enterprise did not come from Great Britain, but from a catastrophic clash with the United States.

Vernet seized three American sealing ships (Harriet, Superior, and Breakwater) for poaching. He arrested their crews and personally sailed the Harriet back to Buenos Aires to stand trial.

The United States government viewed Vernet's actions as piracy. In December 1831, the US warship USS Lexington arrived at Puerto Luis under the command of Captain Silas Duncan. Duncan's crew spiked the settlement's cannons, burned its fortifications, blew up the ammunition stores, and arrested the remaining leadership. They declared the islands completely free of government control and sailed away, leaving the settlement utterly ruined and mostly abandoned.

In late 1832, Buenos Aires attempted to salvage the situation by sending a replacement military governor, but his garrison quickly mutinied. Seeing a power vacuum and a completely exposed archipelago, Great Britain sent the HMS Clio in January 1833 to permanently assert British control.

Vernet’s business assets were briefly managed by his former deputy, Matthew Brisbane, who returned to the islands under British rule. However, in August 1833, a group of disgruntled, unpaid gauchos led by Antonio Rivero launched a bloody uprising, murdering Brisbane and several other top settlers, dealing the final, tragic death blow to the remnants of Vernet's original colony.

That’s an awful claim to sovereignty if you ask me.
